title: Pearson answer format: number-only boxes, typed units, no trailing zeros, leading zeros
blurb: Type every Part A answer in the exact format Pearson marks correct, in both number-only and typed-unit boxes.
question: You calculate 0.8 mL and the stem says "Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place". What exactly should you type?

teach.body: Pearson's rules: some boxes take a number only, usually a whole number but sometimes a decimal; follow any decimal-place instruction; include only significant digits, with no extra zeroes after the decimal point; where a unit is needed, use the standard abbreviation (kg, mg, L, mL) with no added "s", no unit written in full and no extra words. Only an answer in the correct format earns the mark.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice tests page; FACTS.md section 2

teach.h: Worked example: Priya checks her format
teach.body: Priya is practising Part A. Item: 40 mg is prescribed and the ampoule reads 100 mg in 2 mL; "Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place." Volume = 40 ÷ 100 × 2 = 0.8. Typed: 0.8 mL. On the practice test ".9 mL" (no leading zero) was marked wrong, and Pearson warns that 0.80 "may not be shown as correct".

teach.note: On the practice papers these were printed after number-only boxes.

teach.text: Trailing and missing zeros: type 0.8, never .8 (marked wrong on the practice test), and 1.5, never 1.50. In a number-only box, typing a unit or a thousands comma ("600 mg", "2,000") was rejected on entry.

teach.body: The only answer that carries a sign is a fluid balance: +150 mL or -150 mL, as the stem instructs. Every other answer is a plain positive number. Large numbers are typed without commas or spaces: 2250, not 2,250.

items: Number-only box: digits and one decimal point, nothing else.
Typed-unit box: number, space, standard unit (mL, mg, g, kg, L).
Leading zero before a decimal point: 0.8.
No "s", no words, no drug names, no commas.

summary: You can now tell a number-only box from a typed-unit box and type each answer with a leading zero, no trailing zeros and a standard unit. You can also avoid the format slips Pearson marks wrong, such as "mls", unit words and commas.

A.q: You have a prescription for 40 mg. The ampoule label reads 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: 40 ÷ 100 × 2 = 0.8. Typed with a leading zero and the unit: 0.8 mL.

whyNot.1: No leading zero: ".9 mL" was marked wrong on the practice test.
whyNot.2: Trailing zero: the instruction is one decimal place.

A.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 900 mL, IV, over 6 hours. The answer box is followed by the words "mL per hour". What should be typed in the box?
A.why: 900 ÷ 6 = 150. The box takes the number only: 150.

whyNot.0: The unit is already printed; a number-only box rejects letters.
whyNot.1: Trailing zero after a whole number.
whyNot.3: The box accepts digits and a decimal point only.

A.q: You have a prescription for 250 mg. The bottle label reads 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: The stem asks for the unit; a bare number was marked wrong.
whyNot.2: Unit written in full is marked wrong.
whyNot.3: Trailing zero after a whole number.

B.q: A person is advised to drink 2.25 L of fluid a day. The answer box is followed by "mL". What should be typed in the box?

whyNot.0: Commas were rejected by the number-only box.
whyNot.1: The unit is printed already; letters are rejected.

B.q: A tablet strength is 0.075 mg. The answer box is followed by the word "micrograms". What should be typed in the box?
B.why: 0.075 mg × 1000 = 75 micrograms. Type the number only: 75.

whyNot.1: The unit is printed already; letters are rejected.
whyNot.3: Moved the decimal point four places instead of three.

B.q: You have a prescription for 9 mg. The ampoule label reads 25 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.
whyNot.3: Extra trailing zero beyond two decimal places.

C.q: A person weighing 72 kg is prescribed 1.5 mg/kg of a medicine. The ampoule label reads 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

C.q: Convert 500 mg to grams. Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Trailing zero beyond one decimal place.

C.q: A 24-hour chart shows a total input of 2350 mL and a total output of 2475 mL. What is the fluid balance? If the balance is a gain, put + before your answer (for example +100 mL). If it is a loss, put - before your answer (for example -100 mL). Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: No sign: a loss must start with -.
whyNot.2: The stem asks for the unit.

reteach.title: Read the box before you type
reteach.question: A box is followed by "mL per hour" and the answer is 125. What do you type?

blocks.body: If the unit is printed after the box, type 125 and nothing else. If the stem says "Please use the correct unit", type 125 mL. The box tells you which.

blocks.text: Typing the unit into a number-only box is rejected; leaving it out of a typed-unit box is marked wrong.

explain.body: The unit is printed after the box. Type digits and a decimal point only.

test.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 8 hours. The answer box is followed by "mL per hour". What should be typed?

whyNot.1: Trailing zero after a whole number.
whyNot.2: This is the time, not the rate.

explain.body: A value below 1 starts with 0: 0.6, not .6.

test.q: You have a prescription for 30 mg. The ampoule label reads 50 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.2: Trailing zero beyond one decimal place.

test.q: You have a prescription for 125 mg. The bottle label reads 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Trailing zero beyond one decimal place.

explain.body: kg, g, mg, L, mL: no "s", no words, no drug name.

test.q: A person is given two tablets, each containing 2.5 mg. What total dose has been given? Please use the correct unit.
